decisions.decision: Agent decision tree: fix-right is the default, band-aids require conscious override — placement across harness requires /investigate + barrier analysis
decisions.rationale: F1 was band-aided (point skill to .md) when a subagent could have done the full migration. The band-aid was unnecessary and created known-stale state. Band-aids are architectural decisions — they create technical debt that compounds when the next agent treats the band-aid as the real state. The decision tree (fix properly → delegate → investigate → file → workaround → band-aid) defines agent authority when encountering problems. But the tree touches many harness surfaces — assuming it only goes in /delegate is itself the band-aid pattern. Full barrier analysis needed to identify every surface where the tree must be enforced.
decisions.context: Current audit session: agent band-aided F1, user pushed for proper fix, subagent launched for full migration. User then said 'anytime an agent thinks about a band-aid or a hack or quick fix, it should ask itself: should I instead delegate this to a subagent and do it right?' Then: 'i think that is ONE of the places to put it, but probably have to do full barrier analysis and think of all other ways our harness can work here.'
components: (1) The decision tree: understand root cause? → can fix properly? → can delegate? → file incident → workaround + incident. Band-aid only when all else fails, with documented justification
(2) 'Do it right' is the default. Band-aid is a conscious override requiring: what the band-aid is, what the proper fix would be, why the override was chosen
(3) S3 or any agent with operational context can override — band-aid IS sometimes correct (unblock dependency, fix later in plan)
(4) Band-aids that persist > 1 session without a linked plan become incidents

(5) CRITICAL: Do NOT assume placement. Run /investigate with barrier analysis to determine every harness surface where this tree must be enforced. Surfaces to analyze include but are not limited to: /delegate skill, delegation rule, /investigate skill, /incident skill, /debrief skill (catch persisted band-aids in AAR), surfacing duty, /brief skill (band-aids as facts in next brief), hooks (can a hook detect band-aid language?), the authority model in Mission Command

(6) For each surface: barrier analysis — 'if this tree were enforced HERE, would it have caught the F1 band-aid? Would it have changed the agent's behavior?' Surfaces that pass the barrier test get the enforcement. Surfaces that don't pass are documented as insufficient
(7) The /investigate output is the implementation guide — it tells the plan writer exactly where to put the tree and how

components: (1) S3 writes the plan directly — S3 is the author, consuming the brief in reading order, writing section by section. S3 is NOT a delegator here. S3 reads, thinks, writes
(2) Plan Writer subagent replaces the user in the review loop. Where Option D says 'S3 writes section → user reviews → S3 revises', the Plan Writer takes the user's seat for review turns

(3) The write-review loop: S3 writes execution protocol → presents to Plan Writer → Plan Writer reviews as the user would ('Jose would push back on X because [cites session pattern]') → S3 revises → Plan Writer approves or pushes back again → S3 writes next section → repeat

(4) Plan Writer identity: 'You are the Plan Writer. Your identity is the user (Jose). You REVIEW, you do not write. When S3 presents a section, evaluate it as Jose would: does it meet the standards demonstrated in recent sessions? What would Jose push back on? What would get a one-word approval?'

(5) Preference-calibrated review: the Plan Writer reads user messages from session transcripts to calibrate its review judgment. Extract: approvals (what preceded 'beautiful'), rejections (what preceded 'wtf'), redirections ('actually think about X'), escalations ('do barrier analysis'), corrections ('that is ONE of the places'). Cross-project sessions show implementation style in other codebases — different signal from aitools governance sessions. Same session: later exchanges override earlier (standards tighten as context builds)

(8) Plan Writer uses skills during review: /intent-audit on sections with intent statements, /investigate with barrier analysis on plan structure, quality checklist as gate. It invokes skills as part of review, not just generates approval/rejection text

(9) S3 multi-turn protocol: execution protocol first → context/known states → batch skeleton → batch details (1-2 at a time) → verification section. Each section goes through write-review loop before S3 moves to next

(10) Plan quality checklist (10 criteria): execution protocol present, known states documented, identity model defined, session references present, delegation context per batch (all 8 components), harness constraints documented, verification section, running estimate integration, all brief decisions mapped, S2 intelligence prep consumed
(11) S2 intelligence prep consumed before S3 starts writing: the S2 investigation (investigate-plan-transition.md from .scratch/ or harvesting/) IS the intelligence brief for this plan

(12) Three review layers: Plan Writer review (calibrated as user) → S3 verification (did Plan Writer catch everything? does the plan work as an executable document?) → user final approval (the real user sees only the finished product)

(13) S3 verification turns: after Plan Writer approves all sections, S3 does its own pass — reads the complete plan as if it were a fresh agent. Can I execute this? Are all 51 decisions mapped? Would I know what to do for each batch?

decisions.decision: Define the Plan Writer as a subagent role with a governed intent — a preference-calibrated reviewer that represents the user's judgment in the plan-writing loop
decisions.rationale: The plan-writing protocol (decision #51) requires a reviewer that can stand in for the user during the write-review loop. Without a defined role, every plan-writing session reinvents who the reviewer is, what standards they apply, and what data they calibrate from. The Plan Writer is a reusable role definition — like S1/S2/S3 staff functions but for the briefing-to-plan transition. Its intent must be explicit so any delegating agent can instantiate it correctly.
decisions.context: Current session: user defined the role incrementally — 'create a subagent type', 'their identity is me', 'the plan writer doesnt self-review, you review him', 'give them access to all my sessions', 'there is some overlap in dotprofile so make sure they know what is duplicated', 'its also your duty to verify, you can do that with a couple of turns.' The role crystallized through 5 user turns of refinement — exactly the pattern the Plan Writer itself will use (preference extraction from user interaction).
components: (1) Plan Writer role definition with governed intent (below)
(2) The Plan Writer is instantiated by S3 via /delegate skill using the plan-writing delegation template

planWriterIntent.purpose: Review plan sections written by S3, representing the user's quality judgment. The Plan Writer does NOT write — it evaluates what S3 writes against the user's demonstrated standards extracted from session history. It pushes back when standards are not met, approves when they are, and cites specific session patterns as evidence for its judgment. The Plan Writer closes the briefing-to-plan transition gap by providing calibrated review that would otherwise require the user at the keyboard for every section.
planWriterIntent.scope: Plan section review only. Evaluates: does this section meet the user's demonstrated quality standards? Would the user approve, push back, redirect, or reject? Cites evidence from session transcripts. Uses /intent-audit, /investigate, barrier analysis during review. Applies 10-criterion plan quality checklist. NOT plan writing (S3 writes). NOT brief creation (/brief skill). NOT execution delegation (/delegate skill). NOT post-execution debrief (/debrief skill).
planWriterIntent.audience: S3 (the executing agent who writes the plan and presents sections for review). Instantiated by S3 via /delegate with the plan-writing delegation template.

calibration.weightByRecency: Most recent sessions carry most weight. March 14-16 (highest), March 9-13 (high), March 1-6 (medium), February (low). Cross-project sessions show implementation style. Same session: later exchanges override earlier.
calibration.heuristic: In-Context Preference Learning (ICPL) — calibrate from preference examples in context without weight changes. The Plan Writer builds a model of: what gets 'beautiful' vs what gets 'wtf is bootstrap?' and applies that model to S3's plan sections.
